name: The Angel Oak

location.address: 3688 Angel Oak Road, Johns Island, Charleston, SC 29402

access: Free, city-owned park, open 7 days a week (Mon-Sat 9am-5pm, Sun 1pm-5pm), closed holidays. No blankets, drinks, food, props or tripods allowed near the tree; donations welcomed.
transport: On Johns Island, roughly 20-25 minutes by car from downtown Charleston; no direct transit, parking on site
verify_notes: City of Charleston (official, owns the park since 1991) states 300-400 years old, 65 ft tall, 25.5 ft (777cm) circumference, shading 17,000 sq ft. Wikipedia, citing academic estimate, gives 400-500 years, 66.5 ft tall, 28 ft (850cm) circumference, 17,200 sq ft shade, longest branch 187 ft. Sources disagree on exact age band and girth; both are reputable, so age given as the union of both ranges (300-500) and girth recorded from the official city figure. 210th tree registered with the Live Oak Society. Named for the Angel family (Justus Angel and Martha Waight Tucker Angel) who owned the estate, not for any winged-figure legend; local folklore separately tells of ghosts of formerly enslaved people appearing as angels around the tree (Wikipedia; treat as folklore, not fact). Land traced to an 1717 land grant to Abraham Waight; no source says the tree itself was planted then, so do not bridge that date to the tree age. Damaged by Hurricane Hugo in 1989, recovered. Widely but almost certainly wrongly called the oldest tree east of the Mississippi: several bald cypress in the Carolinas are documented older (one in NC over 1600 years, per dendrochronology cited on Wikipedia), so do not repeat the superlative as fact, note it as popular claim. Gift shop sells sweetgrass baskets. Receives approx 400,000 visitors/year.

name: The Cistern Yard Oaks

location.address: 66 George Street, Charleston, SC 29424 (College of Charleston campus)
location.neighbourhood: Downtown Charleston / College of Charleston campus

access: Free, open college campus green, self-guided visits welcome during daylight hours; occasionally closed off for commencement, Spoleto Festival performances or other campus events.
transport: Downtown Charleston, walkable from the historic district; no dedicated transit stop needed
verify_notes: Ensemble entry: a compact, iron-fenced yard of giant live oaks around the 1857 cistern in front of Randolph Hall (built 1828-30, National Historic Landmark), the historic heart of the College of Charleston campus. This is the ensemble everybody photographs (Spanish-moss-draped oaks over the cistern), a single obvious place to stand, treated per the ensemble test as one collectible point rather than an avenue. No individual tree ages found in any source; some of the yard's oaks were lost to Hurricane Hugo in 1989, meaning the current stand includes both old survivors and post-1989 replacements, which is exactly why no age is claimed here (do not bridge the 1785/1857 land history to the trees' planting date, no source makes that claim). Land was a colonial-era military barracks site transferred to the College in 1785; the cistern itself was built 1857. Pin is the yard/landmark centroid (Apple Maps POI for The Cistern Yard), not an individual trunk, hence approximate. Public self-guided campus tours explicitly route visitors here.
